anchors.fact: Michael Jackson (1942–2007) was an English journalist, not the singer. At sixteen he began a series of pieces about pubs for weekly papers in West Yorkshire.
anchors.meaning: An ordinary beginning: pieces about pubs in weekly papers, not a stage. The scale starts small.
anchors.speaksTo: Wren trap: write the scene small · not the singer, one clause

anchors.fact: Apart from a handful of earlier books, publishers hadn't imagined anyone would want to read more about whisky than a label. His 1977 beer book stood out for treating beer thoroughly and seriously.
anchors.meaning: The "before" his work changed: nobody thought there was more to say.
anchors.speaksTo: Wren (4) the "before" · essence: using knowledge to transform the world

anchors.fact: His 1977 *World Guide to Beer* introduced the idea of beer "styles": ways of grouping beers and showing how they relate, like pale ale, porter, pilsner, bock and India pale ale.
anchors.meaning: A way of seeing, not a verdict. Once you know how beers are grouped, you can place one you've never tried, by yourself (our reading, signposted).
anchors.speaksTo: gift: a way of looking, not something to obey · goal: Wisdom

anchors.fact: Ten years later, his *World Guide to Whisky* (1987) did the same for whisky, laying a foundation for a new way of looking at it by showing how the world's whisky types relate to one another.
anchors.meaning: How things relate is what the glass holds: two whiskies from two countries, related (the pair and the link are ours, never his).

anchors.fact: His influence reached writers, readers and drinkers, and just as far among distillers and brewers, many of whom counted him as an inspiration or simply a friend.
anchors.meaning: It spread through people who then used it for themselves.
anchors.speaksTo: fear: being followed into a mistake (inverted) · driver: leave a mark

anchors.fact: Oxford suggests the greatest tribute to his influence is that his books, unique in their day, now seem common and obvious.
anchors.meaning: The word "obvious" is spent here, once, as Oxford's tribute, never as the guest's trait.
anchors.speaksTo: story: make it so simple it seems obvious (spent once)

anchors.fact: No source I read records his doubt, or any check before his styles spread.
anchors.meaning: Signposted only: "I like to think he worried…". Never told as an event.
anchors.speaksTo: fear: a revolution built on a flawed idea · Wren (4), signposted

anchors.fact: Two whiskies called rye, from two countries. Canadian whisky is often called rye, though corn is usually its main grain, with a little rye for flavour. American rye whiskey must be made from at least half rye.
anchors.meaning: Same name, two countries, the grains usually the other way round: a relationship the guest can see at once. The pairing is ours, never his.
anchors.speaksTo: gift: a new way of looking · the drink as proof

anchors.fact: In *The Flavor Matrix*, tamarind sits in the Sour segment of both the Corn chart and the Grain chart.
anchors.meaning: A flavour that goes with both grains, found in a book that charts how flavours relate. The tie to Jackson is our reading (signposted), and the book is about the grains as food, not the whiskies.
anchors.speaksTo: Robin: a spark tied to the story in words

cocktail.closingLine: Put it out there. They'll pick it up with their eyes open.
cocktail.glassware: small tumbler (about 200 ml), chilled in the freezer, no ice
method: Put the tumbler in the freezer for 15 minutes.
Pour both whiskies, the demerara syrup, the tamarind water and the bitters into a mixing glass or a jar.
Fill it with ice and stir quickly for about 15 seconds, until the outside is very cold.
Strain into the cold tumbler. No ice in the glass.
Hold the orange peel over the drink, skin side down, and squeeze it so its oils fall on the top. Rub it once round the rim and drop it in.
cocktail.name: Plain to See

recipe.note: Any blended Canadian whisky made mainly from corn (most are), 40% or a little stronger; not a 100% rye Canadian. Canadian whisky is often called rye, though corn is usually its main grain, with a little rye for flavour.
Any straight rye, 40-55%. This is the one made from at least half rye: the same name, and in a typical bottle the grains the other way round.
Equal parts demerara sugar and hot water, stirred until clear, then cooled.

Break 25 g of sour, seedless tamarind pulp (a block from the world-food aisle; not "sweet tamarind") into a bowl, pour on 60 ml of just-boiled water, leave 30 minutes, mash with a fork and press through a sieve. Keeps a few days in the fridge. Blocks vary: if yours is very sour, use 1 tsp; if it's mild, 2.

cocktail.tagline: You take a yes more seriously than a no.

reading.epigraph: Two countries, two whiskies, both often called rye. One usually holds only a little rye.
whoYouAre: You've seen how something could work better: the way the team runs its week, how the family shares out the holidays, the fix a friend has needed for years. You can see it whole. And before you say a word, you walk back through it, more than once, until you can explain it in a sentence. From outside it looks like confidence. It's closer to care. You know that if they like it, they'll actually do it.
What keeps you up is the yes: everyone's, and then finding out you were wrong. A mistake you make alone stays with you. A mistake people take up because of you travels with every one of them.

So you never hand anyone an answer to obey. You give them a way of seeing it, plain enough to use without you, and to notice if you've slipped. You never asked anyone to believe you. You showed them how to look. That's generosity, and not the usual kind: people leave you more capable, not more in need of you.
yours: In 1977 an English journalist called Michael Jackson (no relation to the singer) published a guide to the world's beer. He'd started at sixteen, writing about pubs for weekly papers in West Yorkshire. His book took beer thoroughly and seriously, and it brought in an idea: beer "styles". Pale ale, porter, pilsner, bock, India pale ale: groups of beers, and how each one relates to the others.

Ten years later he did the same for whisky, with a book that showed how the world's whisky types are related. Before then, apart from a handful of earlier books, publishers hadn't imagined anyone would want to read more about whisky than a label. His influence reached writers, readers and drinkers, and brewers and distillers too, many of whom counted him an inspiration, or simply a friend. Perhaps the best tribute to him is that his kind of book, new in its day, now seems obvious.

Did it ever keep him up at night? I can't say. But I like to think it did, and that it's why his big idea was a way of grouping, not a verdict: with a style in your head, you can place a beer you've never tasted, by yourself. I see you in that. You don't want people simply following you. You want them to see what you saw, and carry on from there without you.

So the cocktail I've made for you is a renowned whiskey classic, an Old-Fashioned, with its whisky drawn from two countries. Canadians often call their whisky "rye", a name from the days when it was wheat whisky flavoured with rye; today most of it is made mainly from corn, usually with a little rye for flavour. American rye whiskey must be at least half rye. Same name, the grains usually swapped, side by side in one glass. To honour his guide to how whiskies relate, I used a guide of my own, a chart of which flavours go together, and looked for a flavour that goes with both grains. I found tamarind, dark and sour, and it gives the drink the sourness it needs to balance. Stirred with ice in a jar, it's strained into a frozen glass with none, and finished with oil pressed from orange peel.

Let me be honest with you about one habit. You keep the next idea back until you're sure, and you'll never feel quite sure enough. But look at what you've already done to it: you've made it simple enough to see through. People who take up an idea like that aren't following blindly. So share it before it's big. A flaw found among a few friends costs a laugh. And if there's no flaw, you get what you were after all along: people doing something better, their own way, because of what you showed them.
